title: You are given an initial capital and a list of projects, each with a capital requirement and a profit. You can complete at most K projects, and completing a project adds its profit to your capital, which can then fund later projects. Choose projects to maximize final capital. Explain the two-heap greedy approach.
shortTitle: Maximize Capital (Two Heaps — Greedy Project Selection)

s1_definition.profdef: Maximize Capital is a Two Heaps problem combining a min-heap keyed by capital requirement with a max-heap keyed by profit. In each of the K rounds, we move every project now affordable with the current capital from the min-heap into the max-heap, then pick the single most profitable affordable project. Adding its profit raises our capital, unlocking more projects next round. The algorithm runs in roughly K log N time plus the cost of the initial heap setup.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the investment desk has a budget and a list of deals, each needing a minimum capital to enter and returning a profit. We can do only K deals. Each deal we close increases our budget, letting us afford bigger deals next. So each round we unlock every deal we can now afford and greedily pick the most profitable one, because taking the biggest profit first grows the budget fastest.
s1_definition.oneliner: Unlock all affordable projects into a profit max-heap, grab the most profitable, bank the profit, and repeat K times.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Maximize Capital is a Two Heaps problem combining a min-heap keyed by capital requirement with a max-heap keyed by profit. In each of the K rounds, we move every project now affordable with the current capital from the min-heap into the max-heap, then pick the single most profitable affordable project. Adding its profit raises our capital, unlocking more projects next round. The algorithm runs in roughly K log N time plus the cost of the initial heap setup.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the investment desk has a budget and a list of deals, each needing a minimum capital to enter and returning a profit. We can do only K deals. Each deal we close increases our budget, letting us afford bigger deals next. So each round we unlock every deal we can now afford and greedily pick the most profitable one, because taking the biggest profit first grows the budget fastest.

**One line to remember:** Unlock all affordable projects into a profit max-heap, grab the most profitable, bank the profit, and repeat K times.

sections.s2_technical:
We sort projects by capital requirement implicitly using a min-heap keyed on required capital, so the cheapest-to-enter projects surface first. Each round, we drain from the min-heap every project whose requirement is at most our current capital and push it into a max-heap keyed on profit. For example, `while (!minCapital.isEmpty() && minCapital.peek().required <= capital) maxProfit.offer(minCapital.poll());`.

Then we take the top of the profit max-heap, which is the most profitable affordable project, and add its profit to our capital. For example, `capital = capital.add(maxProfit.poll().profit);`. If the profit heap is empty at the start of a round, no affordable project remains and we stop early.

A senior-level nuance is why greedy is correct here: once a project is affordable it stays affordable because capital only grows, so deferring it never makes it unavailable, and taking the maximum profit each round provably maximizes capital under the K-project limit. Another nuance is that capital and profit are money, so they are `BigDecimal`, and the max-heap comparator compares profits with `compareTo` in reverse order.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India investment desk starts with a budget and faces a set of deals, each with a minimum capital to enter and a profit on completion. The desk may close at most K deals, and each closed deal grows the budget for the next. The desk wants to end with the largest possible budget. This is exactly how Maximize Capital works: a budget-gated greedy selection.

Problem 2 — Some deals are unaffordable at the start but become affordable after earlier profits land. This is why we keep a min-heap of deals by required capital and move newly affordable deals into a profit max-heap each round, so the choice set grows as the budget grows.

The code defines a `Project` with `BigDecimal` required capital and profit. A `CapitalMaximizer` exposes `maximizeCapital(initial, k, projects)` returning the final `BigDecimal` capital. A `Demo` runs the National Bank of India investment desk through a few rounds and logs each pick.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: initial capital 0, K = 2, deals DealA(req 0, profit 100000), DealB(req 100000, profit 200000), DealC(req 200000, profit 300000).

Step 1: Round one. Capital is 0, so only DealA, which needs 0, is affordable; move it into the profit heap. The profit heap top is DealA with profit 100000, so pick it. Capital becomes 0 + 100000 = 100000.

Step 2: Round two. Capital is 100000, so DealB, needing 100000, is now affordable; move it into the profit heap. DealC needs 200000, still unaffordable. The profit heap holds DealB with profit 200000, so pick it. Capital becomes 100000 + 200000 = 300000.

Step 3: Two rounds are done, the limit K is reached. Final capital is 300000.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Maximize Capital is a Two Heaps greedy problem where I start with some capital and can complete at most K projects, each of which requires a minimum capital to begin and returns a profit that increases my capital. I use a min-heap keyed on the required capital so the cheapest-to-enter projects surface first, and a max-heap keyed on profit so the most profitable affordable project is always on top. In each of the K rounds I move every project now affordable with my current capital from the min-heap into the max-heap, then take the single most profitable one and add its profit to my capital, which unlocks more projects next round.

The reason greedy is correct here is that capital only ever increases, so once a project becomes affordable it stays affordable, and taking the maximum profit each round provably maximizes the final capital under the K-project limit. I also stop early if a round begins with no affordable project, since nothing more can be done.

At the National Bank of India I applied this to the investment desk, which started with a budget, faced deals each gated by a minimum capital and offering a profit, and could close at most K deals, with every closed deal enlarging the budget for the next. I kept all money as BigDecimal, unlocked newly affordable deals into a profit max-heap each round, and greedily closed the most profitable one. Explaining why the two heaps cooperate, one gating by affordability and one ranking by profit, and why the greedy choice is optimal, is what shows an interviewer that I can reason about correctness, not just code a heap.
